grounds.point: M.L. Sharma occupied a portion of the tenanted premises after his employment had ended.
grounds.explanation: Respondents 2-4 stated that M.L. Sharma received the accommodation through his employment and continued residing there after retirement in 1978; his daughter confirmed that he was not employed in 1998-1999 and later died at 40/16. These facts support continued occupation after the employment relationship ended, which is relevant to whether the tenant later parted with possession.

grounds.point: M.L. Sharma's original occupation was permitted by the tenant in connection with his employment.
grounds.explanation: Respondents 2-4 described the accommodation as employment-related, and respondent witnesses testified from company records that M.L. Sharma had been an employee and was permitted to reside there as such. The supplied material therefore supports an initially permissive employee occupation rather than establishing that the initial placement itself was a subletting, assignment or parting with possession.

grounds.point: The tenant later surrendered exclusive possession or control of the relevant portion to M.L. Sharma.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner alleged exclusive possession and parting with possession, while respondent No.1 denied both and maintained that it possessed the premises entirely. Continued residence after retirement is established, but the supplied record contains no identified court finding or sufficiently resolved evidence showing when, if ever, National Insurance ceased retaining legal or practical control over the relevant portion; the reported Delhi precedent confirms the breadth of section 14(b) but does not supply that missing target fact.

grounds.point: Roop Sharma and Rajiv Nanda were themselves given possession of part of the premises by the tenant.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner alleged that Roop Sharma and Rajiv Nanda were in exclusive possession, whereas respondents 2-4 said they were M.L. Sharma's son and son-in-law and only visited him. The supplied evidence confirms those family relationships but contains no resolved finding establishing that either relative independently received possession from the tenant.

grounds.point: Any qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurred without the landlord's written consent.
grounds.explanation: Section 14(1)(b) requires the qualifying transfer of possession to have occurred without written landlord consent, and section 16 likewise treats post-1952 subletting and assignment as requiring written consent. The petitioner alleged absence of written consent, while respondents 2-4 denied that the premises had been given to them without such consent; the supplied record identifies no written consent document or court finding resolving that dispute.

grounds.point: The transfer and vesting of the original New Zealand Insurance tenancy in National Insurance Company independently establishes liability under section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: The record states that the original insurer was nationalized and its tenancy transferred to or vested in National Insurance Company, but the supplied material does not establish this as the pleaded offending transfer. Telesound expressly gives only a prima facie view concerning court-ordered amalgamation and reserves the section 14(1)(b) question, while the reported Parasaram discussion concerns a different liquidation-sale setting; neither resolves the legal effect of this target nationalization or vesting.

reason: The supplied record supports M.L. Sharma's continued occupation after retirement, but it does not resolve the decisive questions whether the tenant actually parted with possession or control and whether any qualifying transfer lacked written landlord consent. On the limited supplied law and evidence, the section 14(1)(b) ground therefore remains undetermined.
